mirroring.label: Mirroring
mirroring.description: Original practice questions authored for the Hansa corpus integration from Microsoft Fabric mirroring documentation harvested by the deep-research corpus. Covers what mirroring replicates and for which sources, how the mirrored copy is stored and queried, replication lifecycle and retention, cost characteristics, CI/CD, and the comparison against shortcuts and pipelines. No video anchors.

questions.title: What mirroring replicates
questions.prompt: Which statement describes what Mirroring does in Microsoft Fabric?

options.text: It continuously replicates a supported source database into OneLake as read-only Delta tables, managed by Fabric.
options.why: Correct. Mirroring is near-real-time, Microsoft-managed replication of supported sources into OneLake Delta.

options.text: It copies tables on a nightly schedule into a warehouse.
options.why: That is scheduled batch copy — the opposite of mirroring's continuous design.

options.text: It creates live pointers to source tables without any local copy.
options.why: That describes shortcuts; mirroring materializes a local copy.

options.text: It streams events into an Eventhouse for dashboards.
options.why: That is the eventstream family, not mirroring.

questions.explanation: Mirroring's definition: managed, continuous replication of supported databases into OneLake as Delta, queried like any lakehouse asset.

questions.title: Open mirroring
questions.prompt: A partner system is not in the supported source list but can write Delta files. Which mirroring capability accepts its data?

options.text: Open mirroring, which lets any application replicate its own data into a mirrored database by writing to the provided landing area.
options.why: Correct. Open mirroring is the documented application-driven replication path.

options.text: A shortcut from the partner's storage.
options.why: Shortcuts reference data in place; they are not the replication path.

options.text: A materialized view over the partner's Delta files.
options.why: Materialized views live in Eventhouses over KQL tables.

options.text: There is no path; unsupported sources cannot enter Fabric.
options.why: Open mirroring exists precisely for this.

questions.explanation: Open mirroring turns the source list into an extensible contract: any producer that can write the expected landing format participates in replication.

questions.title: Why no ETL pipeline

options.text: Fabric manages the replication: change capture from the source, conversion to Delta, and continuous updates are handled by the service.
options.why: Correct. Mirroring is Microsoft-managed end-to-end — the pipeline work is the product.

options.text: Because mirroring only moves metadata, so there is nothing to pipeline.
options.why: Full row data is replicated, not just metadata.

options.text: Because the source pushes files into OneLake nightly.
options.why: That is batch file delivery, not mirroring.

options.text: Because mirroring is only a view over the source.
options.why: A local copy exists in OneLake; it is not a pass-through view.

questions.explanation: The value proposition is precisely the managed replication: capture, conversion and continuous sync are the service's job.

options.text: It stores the raw documents and requires custom parsing in each query.
options.why: The Delta conversion is the product; per-query parsing is not the design.

options.text: It only mirrors the container metadata.

questions.title: Shortcut versus mirror
questions.prompt: A reviewer proposes replacing a mirrored Azure SQL Database with a shortcut to the same tables to save storage. What does that trade away?

options.text: A shortcut references the data in place (queries hit the source path, and there is no managed Delta copy), giving up the local, continuously updated replica mirroring provides.
options.why: Correct. The two features differ exactly there: reference-in-place versus managed local replication.

options.text: Nothing — shortcuts and mirroring are interchangeable for databases.
options.why: They solve different problems; interchangeability is the misconception.

options.text: Shortcuts remove the need for the SQL endpoint.
options.why: Shortcuts do not remove endpoint surfaces; they change where data physically lives.

options.text: Shortcuts replicate data continuously, unlike mirroring.
options.why: That is backwards: mirroring is the replication feature.

questions.explanation: Shortcuts are pointers; mirroring is a managed copy. The storage saved by a shortcut is paid for in query locality and independence from the source.

questions.title: Mirror versus scheduled copy

options.text: The schedule and transformation code disappear: replication is continuous and Microsoft-managed, with the copy kept near-real-time in OneLake Delta.
options.why: Correct. Mirroring removes the scheduled-copy machinery for supported sources.

options.text: The pipeline must still run, now mirroring the pipeline itself.
options.why: That is not a feature; pipelines and mirroring are alternatives for supported sources.

options.text: The data becomes writeable in Fabric.
options.why: Mirrored copies are read-only; write-back is not the design.

options.text: The source must be migrated into the warehouse first.
options.why: Mirroring reads the source as it is.

questions.explanation: For supported sources, mirroring replaces schedule-and-copy plumbing with managed continuous replication — the operational change is the deletion of that plumbing.

options.text: OneLake immediately deletes all replicated tables.

options.text: The replica becomes writeable for manual maintenance.
options.why: The copy stays read-only.

options.text: The source database is detached automatically.
options.why: The source is untouched by stopping.

questions.explanation: Stop means stop syncing: the replica freezes at its last replicated state and remains available — the documented lifecycle behavior.

questions.title: Near real-time, quantified
questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks what 'near real-time' replication means for operational expectations. Which framing matches the documented design?

options.text: Changes replicate continuously as they occur at the source — typically with latency measured in seconds to minutes, not a daily batch window.
options.why: Correct. Mirroring is continuous change replication; the honest expectation is short latency, not batch windows.

options.text: Exactly zero latency — the replica is transactionally synchronized.
options.why: It is asynchronous replication; zero-latency claims would be wrong.

options.text: A fixed hourly cadence.
options.why: There is no fixed cadence; replication is continuous.

options.text: Latency depends on the source's nightly export job.
options.why: No export job exists in the design.

questions.explanation: Near real-time here means continuously applied change replication with short latency — not transactional sync and not batch.

questions.title: Read-only by design
questions.prompt: A planner asks whether analysts can write corrections directly into mirrored tables. What is the documented posture?

options.text: Mirrored data is read-only in Fabric: the replica follows the source, so corrections belong at the source (or in downstream Fabric artifacts, not the mirror).
options.why: Correct. The replica is managed by replication; writing to it would fight the sync and is not the design.

options.text: Mirrored tables accept writes, which replicate back to the source.
options.why: That is bidirectional sync — not mirroring's design.

options.text: Writes are allowed but silently overwritten at the next replication cycle.
options.why: Fabric prevents the write rather than silently discarding it; the posture is read-only.

options.text: Writes are allowed through the SQL endpoint only for admins.
options.why: The read-only posture applies to all principals; it is not an admin exception.

questions.explanation: Mirrored data is a managed, read-only replica: corrections happen at the source, or in downstream Fabric artifacts built on top of the replica.

questions.title: Restarting a stopped mirror

options.text: The missing month replays instantly from the replica itself.
options.why: The replica is the destination; it cannot replay what it never received.

options.text: Resumption is impossible; a new item is always required.
options.why: Resume/re-creation is documented behavior; this absolute is wrong.

options.text: The source must be restored from backup first.
options.why: The source is intact; nothing there needs restoring.

questions.explanation: Long stops are the operational caveat of change-based replication: catching up a month depends on the source's retained change history — plan for re-seed rather than instant replay.
